details: Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS) clinical grading (IAEA EPR-Medical 2018; METREPOL grading): Grade I (Mild; 1-2 Gy whole-body): symptoms: nausea; possible vomiting; fatigue onset; lymphocyte nadir 0.8-1.5 × 10⁹/L (day 7-10); recovery: expected with supportive care; Grade II (Moderate; 2-4 Gy): nausea; vomiting within 1-4hr; diarrhea; fever; hair loss at 2-3 weeks; lymphocyte nadir 0.5-0.8 × 10⁹/L; neutrophil nadir 0.2-0.5 × 10⁹/L (day 21-28); treatment: hematopoietic growth factors (G-CSF; GM-CSF); transfusions; prophylactic antibiotics; Grade III (Severe; 4-6 Gy): vomiting < 1hr after exposure; severe hematopoietic suppression; lymphocyte nadir <0.5 × 10⁹/L; hemorrhage; sepsis; requires ICU + bone marrow transplant consideration; Grade IV (Very Severe / lethal range; >6 Gy): vomiting within 10-30min; watery diarrhea; severe mucositis; neurovascular symptoms (>8 Gy); lymphocyte nadir <0.1 × 10⁹/L; survival uncertain even with BMT; >10 Gy: likely fatal regardless of treatment
current_status_2026: Prodromal syndrome timing vs dose: nausea onset: <30min → dose >6 Gy; 30-120min → 2-6 Gy; >2hr → 1-2 Gy; vomiting: within 10min → >10 Gy; 30min-1hr → 6-10 Gy; 1-2hr → 3-6 Gy; >2hr → 1-3 Gy; this timing = practical dosimetry tool; Chernobyl firefighters: vomiting onset used for triage: vomiting within 1hr → high dose; used to prioritize transfer to Hospital No. 6; biological dosimetry (lymphocyte kinetics): serial CBC measurement every 6-12hr; lymphocyte decline rate and nadir predicts dose ±50%; Guskova formula: dose (Gy) ≈ 4.9 - 2.5 × ln(lymphocyte count at day 7); empirical formula from Chernobyl data; used in first 24-72hr when no other dosimetry available
source: Guskova 2001 J Radiol Prot; IAEA EPR-Medical 2018; ars_cases_REAL.csv; chernobyl_first_responders_medical_REAL.csv

details: Hospital No. 6 (Moscow Clinical Hospital No. 6; Institute of Biophysics): Principal physician: Dr. Angelina Guskova; Head of ARS treatment; facility: 60 ARS-specific beds; specialized radiation medicine facility since 1950s (nuclear weapons program support); established radiation medicine protocols; Patient intake: April 26-27 1986: first 13 patients arrived from Pripyat; within 2 weeks: 134 ARS patients total; triage categories: Grade 1 (1-2 Gy): conservative; Grade 2 (2-4 Gy): hospitalized; hematopoietic support; Grade 3-4 (>4 Gy): ICU; BMT consideration; Treatment strategy: (1) Isolation rooms (sterile environment for immunocompromised); (2) Prophylactic antibiotics (broad-spectrum to prevent opportunistic infection); (3) Antifungal prophylaxis (candida in immunocompromised patients); (4) Transfusion support: RBC transfusions for anemia; platelet transfusions for thrombocytopenia; (5) G-CSF (not available 1986; introduced post-Chernobyl); (6) Wound care for beta burns
current_status_2026: Beta burns: distinct clinical challenge at Chernobyl; firefighters had: (1) Radiation-induced erythema (beta burns to skin from external beta exposure); (2) 'Radiation sunburn' appearance; (3) Progressive: moist desquamation at 2-4 weeks; (4) Secondary infection of beta-burned skin; treatment: topical steroids; wound care; prevention of infection; beta burn area predicts survival: >80% BSA beta burned → fatal; typical patients: 10-40% BSA beta burns; comparison: standard thermal burns protocols adapted; but radiation skin damage HEALS more slowly (impaired stem cell division in skin); Pravik: 20-30% BSA beta burns + bone marrow suppression; died May 1986; treatment was appropriate for era; survival might have been higher with: G-CSF (not available 1986); stem cell transplant with better matching (limited HLA typing capability 1986); modern IL-10 cytokine management

details: Bone marrow transplant (BMT) at Chernobyl: Dr. Robert Gale (UCLA hematologist) arrived Moscow April 30 1986 (invited by Gorbachev via back-channel); 6 days after accident; brought: fresh HLA-typing equipment; international expertise; BMT performed: 13 patients received BMT; outcomes: 2 initial engraftments (18-day and 23-day survival post-BMT); both died: acute complication; ALL 13 BMT patients died; REASON for failure: Guskova finding (which changed international radiation medicine): bone marrow dose threshold: patients who received >6 Gy whole-body had radiation damage not only to bone marrow but ALSO to: gut epithelium (mucosa); lungs; skin; vascular endothelium; transplanted bone marrow ENGRAFTED successfully BUT: patient died from: (1) Beta burns + superinfection; (2) Lung radiation pneumonitis; (3) Multi-organ failure; new marrow could not compensate for non-marrow organ damage
current_status_2026: BMT indication revision post-Chernobyl: Pre-Chernobyl: BMT indicated for any patient with bone marrow failure (>3-4 Gy); Post-Chernobyl Guskova finding: BMT only beneficial if: (1) Whole-body dose 3-7 Gy (range where bone marrow failure is limiting AND other organs can recover); (2) >8 Gy: multi-organ failure dominates; BMT provides no additional benefit; new recommendation: 3-7 Gy: BMT appropriate (with autologous reserve if possible; or HLA-matched donor); >8 Gy: supportive care; palliative if needed; NO BMT benefit expected; this changed global radiation casualty management protocols; REAFFIRMED: Fukushima 2011 (no BMT needed; doses too low); and as general principle in radiation emergency response planning; G-CSF (Filgrastim): licensed for ARS post-2000; mobilizes stem cells; reduces neutrophil nadir duration; would have been given to all Grade 2-3 patients at Chernobyl if available
source: Guskova 2001 J Radiol Prot; Baranov 1989 BMJ; ars_cases_REAL.csv; chernobyl_first_responders_medical_REAL.csv

details: Gastrointestinal ARS syndrome: occurs at >6 Gy whole-body exposure; mechanism: intestinal crypt stem cells (rapidly dividing) → most radiosensitive; crypt cells die → villi denude (mucosal stripping); loss of gut barrier → bacterial translocation → septicemia; clinical: profuse watery diarrhea; bloody stools; abdominal pain; nausea/vomiting; dehydration; sepsis; onset: 3-5 days post-exposure; peak severity: 7-14 days; recovery (if surviving hematopoietic syndrome): depends on stem cell repopulation of crypts (partially possible at 6-8 Gy); at >12 Gy: GI syndrome is fatal regardless of other treatment; Chernobyl data: 28 deaths; many had GI syndrome component; specific patients with documented GI syndrome: Pravik (firefighter; ~6 Gy), Kibenok (~6 Gy): GI syndrome + bone marrow failure; treatment: IV fluids; TPN (total parenteral nutrition); broad-spectrum antibiotics; antifungals; anti-diarrheal medications limited value once crypt damage established
current_status_2026: GI syndrome at Chernobyl: 28 fatalities include patients with: severe GI syndrome (8 patients documented with GI-predominant syndrome); neurovascular syndrome: >15 Gy: CNS + cardiovascular failure within hours-days; not seen at Chernobyl (maximum doses ~15 Gy; all died from hematopoietic + GI combined syndrome); Guskova ARS classification: hematopoietic form (1-6 Gy); gastrointestinal form (6-10 Gy); cerebrovascular form (>15 Gy); combined injury (radiation + burns + trauma = worst prognosis); Chernobyl first responders: most had: combined ARS + beta burns = combined injury; treatment: combines: ARS protocol + burn wound management; prognosis for combined injury: 30-50% higher mortality than ARS alone for equivalent dose; beta burns: prevented adequate wound healing; secondary infection from immunocompromised state; Guskova: 'The skin injuries determined the prognosis more than the bone marrow dose in most of our combined injury patients'
source: Guskova 2001; Turai 2004 Public Health Rev; ars_cases_REAL.csv; chernobyl_first_responders_medical_REAL.csv; stochastic_deterministic_effects_REAL.csv

details: Medical advances in ARS treatment since 1986: (1) G-CSF (Filgrastim; Neupogen): FDA approved 1991; for ARS post-2000 guidelines; stimulates neutrophil production; reduces neutrophil nadir duration by 50%; reduces infectious complications; would have been given to all Grade 2-3 Chernobyl patients; might have saved 5-10 additional patients from infection complications; (2) GM-CSF (Sargramostim): approved; stimulates multiple hematopoietic lineages; (3) Romiplostim: thrombopoietin agonist; increases platelet production; reduces platelet transfusion need; (4) HLA typing: modern molecular HLA typing (microsatellite + SSP) identifies matched donors in hours vs days (1986: serology-based; days to weeks); (5) Stem cell mobilization: peripheral blood stem cells from HLA-matched donor + G-CSF mobilization → higher engraftment rate; (6) GVHD management: tacrolimus + methotrexate → reduces graft-vs-host disease after allogeneic BMT; (7) Romiplostim + G-CSF combined: FDA MCM (Medical Countermeasure) approval 2021
current_status_2026: Medical countermeasures for mass casualty ARS (MCM program): US BARDA (Biomedical Advanced Research and Development Authority): developed MCM for ARS; stockpiled nationwide: G-CSF (Neupogen/Zarxio): strategic national stockpile + push packs for distribution; Amifostine (radioprotector): limited use; severe side effects; romiplostim: approved as MCM; BIO 300 (amiostine analog): Phase 2 trials; PROBLEM for Chernobyl: even with all modern MCMs: patients with >8 Gy whole-body (most Chernobyl firefighter deaths) would still likely die from multi-organ failure; MCM improve survival in 2-6 Gy range; Modern Hospital No. 6 equivalent: every nuclear-capable country now has: radiation emergency hospitals; ARS protocols; MCM stockpiles (IAEA EPR-Medical); IAEA field manual: 'Response to a Nuclear or Radiological Emergency'; updated 2018; distributed to all member states
source: Waselenko 2004 Ann Intern Med; IAEA EPR-Medical 2018; ars_cases_REAL.csv; chernobyl_first_responders_medical_REAL.csv

details: Psychological support for ARS patients: underappreciated component of ARS care; Chernobyl experience: patients knew they had received lethal/near-lethal doses; psychological state: extreme anxiety; awareness of prognosis; isolation (sterile rooms); watched colleagues die; Pravik: age 23 at time of accident; told wife Nadia before dying in Hospital No. 6: 'I may die from this'; documented by Svetlana Alexievich in 'Voices from Chernobyl' (1997); psychological interventions available 1986: minimal (Soviet approach: do not disclose prognosis; Soviet medical paternalism); modern approach: (1) Informed consent (patient told diagnosis and prognosis truthfully); (2) Psychological first aid (PFA): structured support; listening; practical assistance; (3) Clinical psychologist/psychiatrist integrated in ARS treatment team; (4) Family involvement (PREVENTED at Chernobyl: family visits restricted for infection control + information control); (5) Anticipatory grief counseling for high-dose patients
current_status_2026: Hospital No. 6 family contact: wives of firefighters arrived Moscow; held by authorities; allowed limited contact; Alexievich documents: wives smuggled past security to be with dying husbands; received high contamination exposure themselves; several wives: maintained contact despite doctors' warnings → received >200 mSv; one wife (Lyudmila Ignatenko): maintained bedside contact through radiation illness of husband (Vasyl Ignatenko); Vasyl died; Lyudmila: high radiation exposure including fetal exposure (infant born premature; died after 4 hours from multiple organ defects consistent with radiation + prematurity); Alexievich account: most documented case of family radiation exposure at Chernobyl; Lyudmila's own dose: estimated 100-300 mSv; above limit; no confirmed ARS; her daughter (premature birth; congenital defects) → disputed whether radiation-caused or prematurity alone; psychological trauma: lasting

details: REAC/TS (Radiation Emergency Assistance Center/Training Site; Oak Ridge Tennessee): US Department of Energy; global registry of radiation accidents; data: 2714 radiation accidents recorded 1944-2023; total ARS cases registered: 3,048; deaths: 127; categories: criticality accidents (34 events; 60 deaths); lost/stolen source accidents (highest frequency; usually industrial); gamma irradiator accidents; medical overexposure; nuclear power plant accidents (Chernobyl, Goiania, Fukushima; TMI); REAC/TS comparison to Chernobyl: Chernobyl = largest single event in REAC/TS by: ARS cases (134 registered); deaths (28); collective bone marrow dose; Chernobyl context in registry: 134 ARS cases = 4.4% of all global registered ARS cases; 28 deaths = 22% of all registered ARS deaths from single event; Chernobyl + Goiania (1987; 28 ARS + 4 deaths) = 55% of all global ARS cases registered by single events
current_status_2026: REAC/TS case management: provides 24/7 consultation for radiation emergencies; staff: nuclear medicine physicians + radiation physicists; services: (1) Phone consultation for dose assessment; (2) Registry entry for new events; (3) Training for medical personnel; (4) Field deployment for major events; notable REAC/TS activations: Goiania 1987; Tokaimura 1999; Fukushima 2011; in US: industrial source accidents; Chernobyl 1986: REAC/TS had no role (USSR did not request assistance initially; Dr. Gale was independent channel); post-Chernobyl: IAEA-REAC/TS cooperation formalized; IAEA emergency response team = EMERCON (Emergency Response Cooperation); deploys to member states on request; 2022 ZNPP: REAC/TS monitoring; no deployment (access restricted by Russian military)
